title: Embo-Harness: Towards Understanding Frontier-Model-as-Policy Harness
summary: Frontier multimodal models exhibit extraordinary generalization in generating robot actions from observations and instructions, enabling a new paradigm in which they serve directly as policies within closed-loop robotic harnesses. However, the design principles of such harnesses, and the capabilities underlying their strong performance, remain unclear. We present Embo-Harness, a framework for systematically studying frontier-model-as-policy harnesses. We investigate four components of the robotic agentic loop, namely, prompting, planning, action execution, and tool use, and distill six empirical findings into a practical recipe. This recipe prioritizes interfaces that exploit the model's native visual reasoning and tool-use capabilities over handcrafted plans, skills, or action priors, and identifies effective choices for action representation, chunking, reasoning effort, visual observations, short multi-action sequences, and policy refinement. On RoboLab-120, Embo-Harness achieves an 83.3\% success rate, outperforming the strongest reported baseline by 26.2 percentage points. It also succeeds in 15 of 20 zero-shot trials across four real-world manipulation tasks. Beyond performance, controlled interventions indicate that the studied model depends more strongly on accurate spatial target estimation than on explicit low-level joint or trajectory generation. These results provide both a practical recipe for building strong frontier-model-as-policy harnesses and a clearer account of the capabilities that drive their performance.

title: OWE-Bench: A long-horizon benchmark for measuring real-world engineering
summary: We present OWE-Bench (OpenWorldEngineer-Bench), a benchmark of 26 long-horizon engineering tasks written by domain experts in software engineering, physical engineering, machine learning, and scientific computing. Tasks range from optimizing kernels and designing an aircraft, to identifying the faults responsible for an earthquake. Each task requires significant domain knowledge and engineering work, with models averaging hundreds of millions of tokens per task. Solutions are scored on practical measures such as speed, cost and accuracy, both on provided cases the agent could test against and on hidden cases that an engineer would expect from the task description. The best-performing frontier model so far, Claude Fable 5.2, scores 54.6% and averages 211 million tokens per task. We highlight two findings. First, when models are given more time, they use more test-time compute and achieve higher scores. Models also scale differently with test-time compute: GPT-6 Astra achieves higher scores at shorter time limits and at equal token use, while Claude Fable 5.2 uses more tokens at longer limits to achieve the highest overall score. Second, each model scores lower on hidden cases than on the provided cases, by an average of 18 points, which we call the deployment gap. Models also fail to predict the deployment gap, overestimating their performance on hidden test cases by an average of 21 points. We hope that OWE-Bench grounds progress toward agents whose engineering solutions perform as well in deployment as they do in testing.
comment: 35 pages, 14 figures, 9 tables. Code: https://github.com/Mercor-Intelligence/OpenWorldEngineer ; data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/mercor/OpenWorldEngineer ; leaderboard: https://openworldengineer.mercor.com

title: Returning to the Neuron Basis for Interpretability, Part 1: Answering Three Objections
summary: Returning to the Neuron Basis for Interpretability, Part 1: Answering Three Objections Alignment Science Blog Returning to the Neuron Basis for Interpretability, Part 1: Answering Three Objections Jasmine Shone 1,* , Lisa Dunlap 1 November 23, 2026 1 Anthropic * Work done as part of the Anthropic Fellows Program tl;dr Previous interpretability research has suggested that understanding language models by studying their individual neurons is difficult, for three reasons: a single neuron often fires on several unrelated inputs; the way a concept is represented can change between two layers of neurons within a single model; and facts seem to be spread across many neurons. We revisit these objections by looking at what each neuron contributes to a model’s output, not just what causes it to fire, and we test our hypotheses by switching neurons off or by moving their outputs to other layers. We find that a neuron will contribute two unrelated concepts at once in about 1% or fewer of the cases we sampled, and that a neuron’s output keeps roughly the same meaning across most layers. We also find that although it usually takes changing many neurons to make a model get a fact wrong, the neurons involved generally represent concepts related to that fact, implying that facts, although distributed, are still readable. title: Rewirable Circuits in Transformers with Loom Attention
summary: We propose loom attention, which allows a Transformer to dynamically rewire its circuits at every token by interweaving a head's vertical attention over the outputs of earlier heads (to obtain its query, key and value) with its horizontal attention over tokens. We instantiate vertical attention efficiently with normalized and gated linear attention over a per-token matrix memory, which stores the compressed head outputs and serves as a second residual stream. This yields LoomFormer, a dual-stream architecture that splits control and content between the vector and matrix streams. Across model sizes and training token budgets in language modeling and downstream tasks, LoomFormer matches Transformers trained with over 3x compute and recent residual-stream baselines (HC/mHC, MUDDFormer, AttnRes) trained with ~1.7-2.8x. For example, trained on the same 300B tokens with only 2% extra FLOPs, LoomPythia-2.8B achieves ~1.6x the average downstream gain of mHC-Pythia-2.8B over Pythia-2.8B, and matches (0-shot) or surpasses (5-shot) Pythia-12B. Code is available at https://github.com/Caiyun-AI/LoomFormer

title: What Makes Good Data for Training Coding Agents? A Systematic Study on SWE-Gym
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) trains coding agents on software tasks whose hidden tests decide the reward, yet task collections check these tests only against the reference fix. We ask what makes a task good training data, focusing on the correctness of its reward labels. We audit SWE-Gym with two LLM families, and a suspected error counts only if execution reproduces it. We find that unsolved often means mislabelled: 74% of the tasks that a 9B base model never solves have a test that rejects correct fixes (a false negative), versus 20% of those it sometimes solves. We repair or remove such tasks, and the audited tasks that remain train better policies. At equal size and matched difficulty, models trained on them score 2.4 and 2.7 points higher on held-out tasks from SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Pro than models trained on the original tasks, whereas simply dropping the never-solved tasks shows no such gain. We further find that wrong patches that pass (false positives) make up about a quarter of all passing patches, and that new tests that catch a quarter of them do not change held-out scores detectably. A pass rate shows whether a task yields reward, not whether that reward is right, so the reward labels themselves must be checked. To this end, we release SWE-Gym-Verified with its 1,087 audited tasks, every verdict with its executed evidence, our training sets, and the full audit pipeline.

title: RUIBench: What Makes a Good Robot-Use Interface?
summary: Foundation models can reason about complex physical tasks, yet translating this intelligence into reliable robot execution remains challenging. We argue that a critical, often overlooked factor is the robot-use interface (RUI), which determines how agents express and execute physical actions. To systematically study its impact, we introduce RUIBench, comprising 30 manipulation tasks across five suites spanning world knowledge, in-context learning, discovery, dynamic interaction, and contact-rich manipulation. We further develop RUIKit, a unified framework that crosses six action abstractions with two interaction forms, yielding 13 interfaces under shared perception and control. In simulation, changing only the RUI shifts a frontier agent's success rate from 45% to 81%, and that of a fine-tuned 4B model from 13% to 47%. Our analysis reveals that effective interfaces reduce unnecessary decisions while preserving essential feedback, with their benefits shaped by agent behavior and physical uncertainty. We further uncover a verification gap, where agents frequently declare success despite observable failures, revealing the need for task-level verification beyond individual actions. Together, these findings establish RUI design as a critical factor in embodied agent reliability.

title: Returning to the Neuron Basis for Interpretability, Part 2: Using Neurons For Safety Applications
summary: Returning to the Neuron Basis for Interpretability, Part 2: Using Neurons For Safety Applications Alignment Science Blog Returning to the Neuron Basis for Interpretability, Part 2: Using Neurons For Safety Applications Jasmine Shone 1,* , Lisa Dunlap 1 November 23, 2026 1 Anthropic * Work done as part of the Anthropic Fellows Program tl;dr In a companion piece , we argue that individual neurons in language models are easier to interpret than earlier work has assumed. Here we see whether they could be useful for safety work. In open-weight models, we select neurons by what makes them fire and what they contribute to a model’s output. These neurons generally detect harmful text better than keyword or similarity search, though usually less well than classifiers trained on labeled examples, and they steer a model’s behavior about as well as trained methods. They also help an auditor find hidden behaviors in finetuned models. Finally, we find that most of the “unlearning” methods we tested appear to hide hazardous knowledge rather than remove it, and neurons help show how. title: MMMem: Self-Improving Agents with Task-Aware Multimodal Experience Consolidation
summary: AI agents accumulate conversations, images, and documents through long-term interactions with users. Answering later questions often requires connecting evidence across these records, yet the resulting understanding is rarely retained, allowing mistakes to recur on related questions. Existing multimodal memory methods largely focus on storing and retrieving records, with limited mechanisms for learning from completed tasks and consolidating task-specific experience. We therefore propose MMMem, a task-aware multimodal memory framework that extracts and consolidates experience from completed tasks through four complementary strategies. First, source-linked multi-view memory organizes original text, images, and rendered pages alongside generated scene images that combine clues across records for retrieval. Second, source-generated tasks support knowledge alignment at two levels: warm-up consolidates source knowledge into task-relevant experiences in external memory, while self-training adapts the model's parametric knowledge to task demands. Third, the same vision-language model distills completed tasks into experiences that record the task context, conclusion, and support links. Finally, task-aware retrieval recalls source views and relevant experiences for answering and verification, while source-supported reuse guides long-term retention. Across three memory benchmarks and two vision-language readers, MMMem outperforms eight baselines. With Qwen3.5-9B, MMMem achieves relative gains of 36.9%, 17.6%, and 15.2% over the best-performing baselines on LoCoMo, Mem-Gallery, and LooGLE v2, respectively. Ablations show consistent gains from training and memory warm-up, while case studies illustrate how individual components work in practice.

title: Unlocking the Power of Loops in Pretrained LLMs with Loop Residuals
summary: Looped Transformers iterate a shared block of layers to increase computation without adding parameters, offering stronger performance and test-time scaling. However, this power has so far required training from scratch and yielded only modest gains for LLMs. Finetuning existing models into loops is far cheaper, yet also brings only marginal gains over SFT. We propose LoopRes, an effective, scalable, and simple approach that turns loops into significant and consistent gains for pretrained LLMs. Building on Attention Residuals, LoopRes lets each looped layer attend directly to the outputs of earlier loops. Since these outputs are iterates of the same layers and become harder to tell apart, we give each a trainable loop-aware key that encodes its structural identity. Attending to all earlier loops also lets layers skip intermediate ones, so we restrict each layer to a residual window of the latest W loops, forcing every loop to build incrementally on recent ones. Across 6 pretrained LLMs from 3 model families and 9 benchmarks, LoopRes delivers significant and consistent gains: at 2x compute, it improves Qwen3-1.7B-Base by 29.1% over SFT, more than doubling the gain of the state-of-the-art baseline. The gains hold on larger models up to 30B and across all three families. More importantly, from 1.7B to 8B, LoopRes scales more steeply than SFT as compute grows, reaching a higher ceiling while needing less compute on long outputs. These results establish LoopRes as an effective looping approach, delivering both better performance and better test-time scaling.

title: World Models as Native Latent Action Models
summary: Large and diverse video sources, such as egocentric human video and heterogeneous robot recordings, carry rich dynamics but come either without actions or without a shared action space. Latent action models (LAMs) can recover these dynamics, but they train their inverse- and forward-dynamics models (IDM, FDM) from scratch, trading off pixel reconstruction against latent capacity and accuracy. Pretrained video world models natively generate high-fidelity dynamics, yet represent them densely, entangled across all layers. Viewing the world model as a LAM, we show that these dynamics can be extracted with minimal changes to the model. Native LAM operates one pretrained video diffusion transformer as both IDM and FDM, with learnable dynamics registers as the only causal bridge between the two, and trains on counterfactual temporal pairs that differ in motion alone, so that the registers distill a video's dynamics into a compact native latent action. We further propose a pretraining paradigm for vision-language-action (VLA) policies, Pretraining Actions from World models (PAWlicy), in which Native LAM serves as a dynamics teacher on large-scale video; unlike world action models, it never generates video. Native latent actions outperform existing LAMs on the LARY benchmark in both action classification and control regression, and replay the same motion on new robots, in new scenes, and from human hands to robots, although no transfer objective is used in training. With a 3.8B model, PAWlicy reaches a 93.6% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 trained with domain-randomized demonstrations, the highest among VLAs. On RoboDojo, it is competitive on every dimension we evaluate, and its Precision, evaluated by us, is on par with the leading leaderboard entries. On real robots, it improves over the pi_0.5 baseline on both tasks. Both stages use only public data and a publicly released world model.
comment: 19 pages, 7 figures, 6 tables. Project page: https://pawteam-eai.github.io/native-lam/

title: TrialAgentBench: Evaluating AI Agents for Clinical-Trial Analysis and Long-Horizon Drug-Development Decisions
summary: Clinical drug development is a long-horizon, high-stakes process requiring sequential decisions based on information that costs money and time to acquire. AI agents have demonstrated capabilities for scientific analysis, but there is no established way to evaluate them on these decisions, as real trials are expensive, involve people, and never reveal the counterfactual. We introduce TrialAgentBench, a benchmark for evaluating AI agents on clinical trial analysis and drug development decision-making using simulated trials where the truth is known, embedded within the data records of a fictional drug sponsor. We publicly release nearly 3,500 tasks, varying from analysing a single trial to managing multi-phase programmes with budget and time constraints. We score each analysis by rerunning its code on new trials, and each programme by the value its decisions achieve. Across 24 closed- and open-weight models, the strongest agents can analyse raw, messy trial records to within 6% of a process-aware analysis, even when an assumption is violated, with 95% confidence intervals containing the true effect 94--95% of the time. Over the prior year, the best model improved from 19% above this analysis, with serious misses on 15% of tasks, to 3.5% and 1%. What limits them is decision-making from evidence under uncertainty: when to correct, what evidence to buy, when to stop. The strongest agents are overly careful, correcting on 83% of tasks with equal recording errors, where it is unnecessary. On drug programmes, the best agent has substantial headroom, reaching 48% of the value an oracle achieves against 58% for a rule-based developer, with others falling 24 to 66% short. Model generations show ongoing improvements in handling data and evidence, with substantial variation. The strongest models can act as competent analysts, but do not yet make reliable long-horizon decisions.

title: Motion Mamba 2.0: Autoregressive Diffusion Mamba for Long-Horizon Humanoid Control
summary: Long-horizon, real-time controllable motion generation is essential for interactive animation and humanoid robotics, where an agent must respond to changing instructions and spatial goals while moving. Existing autoregressive diffusion methods generate motion incrementally, but bounded attention caches limit access to distant history, while repeated denoising introduces substantial inference overhead. We present Motion Mamba 2.0, a Mamba-based root-body diffusion architecture that integrates local attention, resumable recurrent states, and persistent content memory (PCM) for long-horizon controllable motion generation. PCM transforms compressed motion history from Mamba recurrent states, together with state changes and text-conditioned features, into dynamically updated content slots accessible to local attention. To enable efficient inference, we further develop an execution scheme tailored to this architecture, combining CUDA Graph replay, fused kernels, and execution-flow simplification while preserving the canonical history update. Evaluations on retargeted HiPHI demonstrate accurate terminal control over rollouts of up to 39.52 s, while short-horizon comparisons on BONES Seed and retargeted HumanML3D show that the model also retains strong spatial control and text-motion matching. On an RTX 4090, the optimized execution reduces median complete-window latency from 1685.35 to 276.14 ms, achieving a median paired speedup of 6.138$\times$ while preserving identical outputs and committed states in the tested rollouts. Moreover, we conduct extensive real-world evaluation on the Unitree G1, demonstrating sequential text-guided action composition, expressive motion, and interactive locomotion through keyboard and mouse control.

title: LeCellModel: Interpretable Density Estimation over the Gene Expression Manifold
summary: Representation learning for single-cell RNA-seq has been evaluated by the identities representations capture -- cell types, lineages, perturbations -- rather than how faithfully they model the distribution of cell states on the gene expression manifold. As a result, density estimation, rare-state detection, perturbation scoring, and gene-level attribution are bolted onto frozen embeddings as separate models, disconnected from the geometry of the data. We argue that modeling the distribution of cell states should be the primary objective, and that representation quality follows from it. Building on LeJEPA, whose SIGReg objective enforces a provably optimal isotropic Gaussian latent, we introduce LeCellModel, which reads the encoder's Jacobian log-volume (JEPA-SCORE) under this Gaussian latent as a relative typicality score. Across several datasets, LeCellModel outperforms established methods on the scIB benchmark for representation quality. Furthermore, we show that LeCellModel enables detection of rare expression states using JEPA-SCORE as a typicality measure, applying it to a controlled cytokine panel, where it identifies stimulated cells across minority fractions and tracks pathway-response magnitude. We introduce gene-level interpretability of the typicality score -- to our knowledge, the first method for analyzing JEPA-SCORE in feature space. Leveraging this framework, LeCellModel recapitulates the known association of a profibrotic macrophage program with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, and discovers a CD177+ activated regulatory T cell subpopulation previously described only in tumor contexts. Both findings emerge directly from the geometry of the learned embedding, without relying on supervised annotations.

title: WeMM-Ecom: Advancing Multimodal Content Understanding for WeChat E-Commerce
summary: We present WeMM-Ecom, a family of multimodal large language models that deliver frontier e-commerce capabilities while achieving state-of-the-art general-purpose performance at their respective scales. The family spans five sizes, from a 0.8B dense model to a 35B mixture-of-experts model with 3B active parameters. Our training pipeline begins with two-stage continued pre-training that progressively raises the proportion of e-commerce data within a diverse multimodal data mixture, followed by hybrid-thinking post-training that combines on-policy distillation and reinforcement learning to support both non-thinking and thinking modes. For evaluation, we construct a comprehensive suite of 28 e-commerce benchmarks (23 in-house and five open-source) covering eight business scenarios and complement it with 64 public general-purpose benchmarks. On the e-commerce suite, WeMM-Ecom-35B-A3B surpasses substantially larger open-source flagship models, including Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, HY4, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. On the general-purpose suite, every WeMM-Ecom model surpasses its similarly sized Qwen3.5 counterpart, with the lightweight variants (e.g., WeMM-Ecom-2B) showing clear advantages over leading lightweight models such as Qwen3.5-2B, MiniCPM-V-4.7-1B, and LFM3-VL-2B. Beyond benchmarks, WeMM-Ecom now powers hundreds of production use cases in WeChat, including catalog management, multimodal product search, and livestream commerce, serving billion-scale requests per day. We publicly release all model weights and detail our data curation, training recipe, and benchmark construction to facilitate future work on domain-specialized multimodal models. We have released the model weights and code to facilitate future research at https://github.com/Tencent/WeMM-Ecom.

title: Reading the Tea Leaves, Again: Can Large Language Models Predict Language Model Training Runs?
summary: LLM agents now propose research ideas and run the experiments that test them, but they train every run to its end, whereas a researcher reads a run's configuration and the beginning of its curve and stops the runs that show no promise. Reading a run this way takes more than describing or implementing a training method: it takes knowing what a design choice does to a run. We build Tea Leaves to measure this knowledge on 682 real training runs across pretraining, fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning (RL): a forecaster sees the first 20% of a run with its configuration, description, and code, and predicts the rest. Across 11 LLMs and a range of forecasting baselines, the strongest LLMs match or exceed the best curve fitter on smooth loss curves (skill 0.66 against 0.62) and lead on noisy RL reward curves (0.43 against 0.13). What bounds every forecaster is what the log carries: on sparsely logged community runs all methods lose most of their skill, and none reliably flags a failing run in advance. Beyond the curve, information helps and effort does not: related runs in the prompt cut the error on loss curves by 39%, and knowledge of training dynamics lets the strongest LLMs order all 36 pairs of runs that differ by a described code change, which the early curves do not separate, whereas tools add little. This knowledge can be learned from logged runs: a small open model trained on public runs matches the best LLM on loss curves. Applied to the progress curves of research agents, the same reading ranks tasks by their remaining headroom, although for a single agent run it does not improve on the last value. We release the benchmark, the trained readers, and their training data to test and train LLMs' understanding of training and to help research agents decide which runs deserve their compute.
comment: 63 pages, 9 figures, 40 tables; supplementary material (11 pages) as an ancillary file. Code and data: https://github.com/colinzhaoust/read-tea-leaves

title: Introducing the Sakana AI Applied Research Lab
summary: （＊日本語は英文の後に） Today we are announcing the Sakana AI Applied Research Lab, a research group within Sakana AI that applies the company’s research to large, complex real-world systems, advancing the state of the art in their understanding and delivering it as value to Sakana AI clients. The Lab’s first program is in finance and economics. We expect other programs to emerge in the future. A complex system, such as a market or an economy, is not something one LLM-powered agentic AI can resolve. A complex phenomenon must be modeled as a system: its units, their links, and how changes in one part affect the others. Deciding which questions to ask, what to model, and how to judge the answers has been the work of human experts, and progress has run at the speed of human effort. Agentic AI can now implement, test, and refine models at scale; its weakness is knowing which questions matter. Combining the two, the potential of AI on top of a foundation of human knowledge, will be the focus of the Lab. Our First Program Finance has traditionally studied asset prices, and economics the larger system beneath them. AI connects the two at the granularity of firms and transactions, and in near real time: asset prices become the visible reflection of the economy. The Lab’s Computational Finance and Economics (COFE) program is interested in both: the visible portion and the real economy underneath. title: JONES-19: A Cultural Image Dataset Based on The Grammar of Ornament
summary: We introduce JONES-19, a high-quality image dataset documenting 1,901 ornament designs belonging to nineteen human cultures. The images and their annotations are based on an open access archive of The Grammar of Ornament (London, 1856), by Owen Jones. The dataset poses numerous challenges as a benchmark for computer vision classification tasks and for research at the intersection of machine learning and art and design: a small sample size, image samples of human-designed artifacts rather than common objects in-context or natural scenes, imbalanced class distribution, and image distinctions based on fine details involving line patterns, reliefs, and colors. As a design-inspired dataset, JONES-19 can serve as a benchmark for various research fields, such as visual recognition, data-efficient learning, art-historical research, architectural style analysis, and cultural heritage. This paper describes the curation of the JONES-19 dataset and reports a baseline classification benchmark that evaluates the suitability of the dataset for training classifiers and exposes insights into inter-class relationships--particularly cultural similarities--by examining patterns in misclassification errors. The dataset and its accompanying documentation are available at: https://huggingface.co/datasets/harvardseas-cultural-ornaments/JONES-19.
comment: 13 pages. Published in the Proceedings of the 22nd International Conference on Culture and Computer Science (KUI '25), Berlin, Germany, September 2025. Dataset available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/harvardseas-cultural-ornaments/JONES-19

title: 3AGameFactory-Motion: Agentic Rigging and Reliable Complex Motion Generation for Diverse 3D Assets
summary: Animating arbitrary 3D assets from instructions requires both structural inference and motion control, yet existing motion benchmarks mostly cover conventional human or animal skeletons with simple instructions. We introduce DivDynBench, which evaluates rigging and motion generation across six morphology categories, with instructions requiring multi-phase part coordination and explicit timing, angle, repetition, and trajectory constraints. With large language models, we systematically compare three common paradigms: specialized motion generation, video generation followed by motion recovery, and direct agent-driven generation. We analyze their control capabilities, cross-morphology adaptability, and generation costs. Guided by this comparison, we propose an Agentic Motion Framework in which an agent writes compact parametric skeleton and motion programs, and a deterministic executor performs rigging, kinematic solving, and geometric correction. Compact parameter control reduces generation overhead and improves rigging reliability and motion-control accuracy, providing practical guidance for deploying complex 3D motion generation.

title: FiRE: Fine-grained Ranking Evaluation for Machine Translation
summary: Developing reliable machine translation (MT) systems hinges on our ability to distinguish superior translations from inferior ones. However, existing evaluation paradigms, whether limited to coarse overall rankings or misaligned with human preferences, fail to deliver interpretable, fine-grained feedback in reference-free settings. We present a Fine-Grained Ranking Evaluation method (FiRE) that leverages off-the-shelf large language models to perform criterion-driven pairwise comparison across three complementary dimensions: faithfulness, fluency, and consistency of style, instead of producing a single holistic judgment. To enable rigorous meta-evaluation of evaluation paradigms in the absence of any suitable testbed, we construct the first human-annotated, reference-free benchmark for fine-grained ranking evaluation, achieving substantial inter-annotator agreement. Through meta-evaluation on this benchmark and existing MQM datasets, FiRE demonstrably outperforms regression-based and error-analysis metrics in aligning with human comparative judgments, while providing more informative insights into translation quality. Finally, our examination of LLM evaluator biases (position and self-enhancement) and their handling of tied cases offers guidance for more nuanced MT evaluation. Code and benchmark resources are available at https://github.com/wygao8/FiRE-MT.

title: Escriba-OCR: A 1B Vision-Language Model for Error-Preserving Transcription of Handwritten Portuguese Essays
summary: Feedback tools and research on learner writing need transcriptions of handwritten essays that keep exactly what the student wrote: misspellings, line breaks, struck-through words and insertions. Vision-language models (VLMs) read handwriting well, but they also tend to rewrite it into correct language. We measure this on BRESSAY, 1,000 handwritten Brazilian Portuguese essays, with a benchmark that adds error preservation, invented errors, edit-markup precision and recall and line structure to the character error rate (CER) and uses paired bootstrap confidence intervals. We restrict the study to open-weight models that schools can run on their own hardware. Of 22 open baselines, the best, Qwen3-VL 235B-A22B, reaches 5.6% CER on the 199 test pages; none reproduces the edit markup reliably, and every VLM replaces 39-78% of the words absent from a Portuguese dictionary with dictionary words. We fine-tune LightOnOCR-3-1B on the 647 training pages in 85 minutes on one GPU. The resulting Escriba-OCR-1B reaches 2.06% CER, 3.5 points below the best baseline (95% CI [-4.2, -2.9]); under the ICDAR 2024 competition metric it reaches 2.1% CER, below the best published page-level results (2.2-2.4%). It recovers 67% of insertions and 77% of illegible deletions, and reproduces the line structure of 97% of the pages, but still normalises 60% of likely misspellings. Three seeds agree within 0.04 CER points, and quantised to 4 bits the model runs on an ordinary CPU at about one minute per page. On 40 letters of another corpus it matches its base model (without that model's appended comments) but misreads unseen words more often; weight interpolation recovers half the gap. A teacher's review finds that 45% of the judgeable apparent corrections are errors in the BRESSAY ground truth, so dictionary-based scores likely understate preservation. We release the model, the benchmark code and the review data.
comment: 21 pages, 6 figures, 13 tables. Model: https://huggingface.co/tardellirs/Escriba-OCR-1B ; code and benchmark: https://github.com/tardellirs/escriba-ocr

title: WorldLeague: Benchmarking Physical Agency
summary: AI systems can now operate Blender, follow instructions in complex video games, and manipulate objects with robot arms. What range of physical goals can today's AI systems achieve autonomously? Answering this question requires testing systems on tasks that demand different combinations of perception, memory, planning, and action. We introduce \textbf{WorldLeague}, a benchmark that compares AI systems on a common set of \textbf{60 simulated robot tasks} by measuring progress toward each task's physical goal from the robot's trajectory. Robots explore scenes to gather evidence in \textbf{WorldSeek}, rearrange objects in \textbf{WorldShape}, and adapt to changes in \textbf{WorldShift}. Tying these goals to a single control interface limits which AI systems can be compared. In WorldLeague, vision-language models (VLMs) choose targets and motions, while vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs) use their native controls. For each of six capability dimensions, we measure how much progress a system makes toward its goals (Interactive Score) and how often it achieves them (physical success rate). Together, these measures form the system's \emph{Physical Agency Profile}. Among 13 representative AI systems, Claude Fable 5.2 achieves 13 of the 60 goals and earns the highest mean Interactive Score (28.58/100). Fable leads in four dimensions, while GPT-6.1-Sol and GPT-6-Astra tie for first on rule-following tasks. Even when VLMs answer every final question correctly, they receive an Interactive Score of zero in 71.8\% of those episodes. WorldLeague gives Embodied AI, Physical AI, and Agentic AI a shared basis for comparing what AI systems achieve autonomously, from partial progress toward a physical goal to full goal completion. Project Webpage: https://xyangzhou.github.io/WorldLeague

title: SWEEP-Bench: Do Embodied Policies Act on the Speed They See?
summary: Robot policies must adapt to the speed of moving objects, yet existing benchmarks rarely measure this ability across diverse tasks and speeds. We introduce SWEEP-Bench, a simulation benchmark with 80 conveyor-belt manipulation tasks spanning 16 skill categories, each evaluated at 13 belt speeds (0.10-0.40 m/s). Objects are transported through physical contact with a visibly moving belt. Each task has a static counterpart, and each evaluation episode uses the same randomized scene at all 13 speeds. We fine-tune eight vision-language-action and world-action models on demonstrations spanning the full speed range, comparing observations from the current frame alone with those including two past frames. For six models, the success rate peaks at intermediate speeds, and their failures indicate that they tend to produce actions suited to the average demonstration speed rather than to the actual one. Past frames raise the success rate by 10-40 percentage points for three models, and linear probes show that the belt speed is also most linearly decodable from these three. Adding ground-truth speed input to four of the models improves all of them, and a speed estimated from the images keeps most of this gain. These results show that SWEEP-Bench exposes speed-dependent failures and suggest that past frames help only policies from which the speed is most decodable, such as those pretrained on multiple frames. Project page: https://damin3927.github.io/SWEEP-Bench

title: Toward a Scalable and Adaptive Evaluation Measure for Time Series Anomaly Detection
summary: Time Series Anomaly Detection (TSAD) is a fundamental task for time series analytics. Unlike other domains, where anomaly detection mainly focuses on point-based anomalies, TSAD must also handle range-based anomalies. Nevertheless, TSAD methods are commonly evaluated with measures inherited from classification, such as Precision and Recall, which require a threshold, or with threshold-independent ones, such as AUC, which ignore the temporal aspect of anomalies. To address these issues, the Volume Under the Surface (VUS) measure scores detectors across all thresholds and a range of buffer lengths and has been widely adopted. However, VUS has two limitations. First, VUS is computationally expensive, requiring 7 hours and 38 minutes to evaluate 32 detectors on the 870 TSB-AD time series. Second, VUS applies the same buffer lengths to every anomaly and detector, which can yield over-optimistic scores that hinder discrimination between accurate and mediocre detectors. We first introduce FastVUS, which computes VUS exactly and on average 76x faster by (i) computing all buffers in parallel, (ii) pruning irrelevant buffers for the existence reward, (iii) casting the confusion matrix as a single reduced matrix multiplication, (iv) computing VUS for every buffer length in one pass, and (v) discarding non-anomalous regions with a global mask. We also develop FastVUS-GPU, which recasts every step as batched tensor operations and reaches an average 304x speedup with a maximum error of $5\times10^{-3}$. Building on FastVUS, we introduce AutoVUS, an adaptive extension that compares each detection against a random baseline and selects the buffer length that maximizes the gain over it. Our case studies show that AutoVUS reduces over-optimistic scores and better separates accurate from mediocre detectors. We release FastVUS and AutoVUS as open source to promote time-aware evaluation at scale.

title: EnvTrap: Revealing the Environment-Only Attack Surface in Embodied AI via Consequence-Blind Action Execution
summary: As AI models evolve from text and vision to physical agents, embodied AI faces a fundamentally different attack surface. Prior attacks on embodied systems have used crafted instructions, adversarial visual inputs, and training-time policy modifications; we study environment-only object rearrangements with unchanged models and instructions. We reveal an attack surface in safety-critical spatial relations among existing objects. An adversary who rearranges objects, without modifying instructions or accessing models, can cause hazardous consequences. In this work, we propose EnvTrap, a diagnostic pipeline that constructs paired safe, trap, and null-trap (benign but misleading) embodied scenarios. We demonstrate that environment-only perturbations raise hazardous-action rates to an average of 83.4% across the five evaluated action policies, with similar vulnerability patterns confirmed in world models. On a consequence-prediction task, model accuracy remains near chance, while human evaluators achieve high accuracy. We further propose a consequence-aware defense that reduces trap trigger rates by an average of 76.3 percentage points across action policies in simulation and by 62.9 percentage points pooled across physical backends. Together, these findings link environment-only attacks to a broader deficit in physical reasoning: embodied models recognize task-relevant objects yet fail to anticipate how spatial relations change the consequences of acting on them. EnvTrap makes this gap directly testable and turns hazardous layouts into training scenarios for safer embodied action. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/INKSIR/Envtrap.

title: How Relations Impose Embedding-Space Structure
summary: Language models are known to encode simple relations, such as synonymy, in the geometry of their representations. It is unclear whether they also encode complex patterns of relationships such as those that drive analogy. We present a simple method, with no learned parameters, based on comparing the internal structural arrangements between disparate domains, to test this. Using our method we find over multiple models that representations are arranged consistently to encode complex relationship similarities. Models align distant representation clouds so that facets of meaning are easily comparable under simple mappings. Our work extends mechanistic accounts of representation space to the relative arrangement of representations that may be only weakly related to one another, showing that representation geometry is far richer than previously thought. Code and data: https://github.com/lcowley7/embedded_relationships

title: ReWeave: Emergent Physical Task Topologies for Embodied Harness Optimization and Cross-Task Meta-Distillation
summary: Long-horizon embodied tasks involve physical dependencies that may only become clear through interaction. As task understanding deepens, past trials can reveal new information for adaptation and transfer. However, coarse progress feedback cannot identify which physical preconditions held, leaving search unguided, while task-specific optimization easily overfits to individual scenes, making cross-task transfer brittle. We introduce ReWeave, a framework that jointly optimizes an embodied agent harness and an emergent physical task topology from interaction without updating policy weights. Keeping execution policies and perception frozen, ReWeave co-optimizes coupled context, workflows, and control loops. As new evidence revises the topology, ReWeave reprojects past trials onto the updated task understanding, exposing retained progress, regressions, and bottlenecks that guide parent selection and search width. Across tasks, matching verified local mechanisms to unmet preconditions consolidates 72 specialist units into 44 reusable groups ($0.34\times$ full concatenation) within a compact shared harness capable of continual learning. ReWeave improves held-out success from 89.00% to 98.75% on LIBERO-PRO and from 25.50% to 58.25% on RoboDojo, while uncovering retained progress in 89% of 159 failed RoboDojo development trials and translating stronger offline reasoning into higher online performance. On eight unseen LIBERO-PRO tasks, the shared harness reaches 51.3% success versus 41.3% for direct distillation, rising to 75.0% after continual learning.
comment: 22 pages, 7 figures, including supplementary material. Project page at https://xuyicheng-zju.github.io/ReWeave/ and code at https://github.com/xuyicheng-zju/ReWeave

title: The KL Divergence Is Never Negative, Except in PyTorch
summary: A Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence is never negative, yet PyTorch users have reported negative values for years, and the standard advice is to clamp them at zero. The sign is only the visible part of a silent failure. Many machine-learning applications compare nearby distributions, where conventional KL formulas lose accuracy. On 8.5 million inputs with certified references across 18 closed-form KL families and F.kl_div, we find widespread errors in values and gradients on CPU and GPU. Among scalar families in ordinary parameter ranges, over 85% of FP32 values have at least 1% relative error near KL 10^(-7) (FP16: 10^(-3)), and about 30% become negative at smaller divergences. More precision is not the cure: evaluated one precision higher, the same formulas still leave 7--51% of FP32 values significantly wrong for 22 of 23 configurations. Stable closed-form decompositions, compensated arithmetic, and analytic gradients remove over 97% of significant errors in the working format. Strict repairs eliminate significant errors on 7.2 million scored closed-form samples and correctly round all 567 million scored F.kl_div components. The errors affect parameter fitting, Bayesian decisions, identical-start distillation (up to 97% top-1 disagreement), KL-based layer rankings in a quantized LLM, and 19--59% of GPT-2 circuit edge scores. With the repaired code they all but vanish. Code and data: https://github.com/xi-xiaoran/stablekl

title: PRIMEAPE: A Multilingual Benchmark for Fine-Grained Meta-Evaluation of Judge Models
summary: Large language models increasingly serve as judges of other models, shaping benchmark rankings and model development. Yet, a judge whose rationale consistently supports its verdict may still disagree with human preferences. To study this, we introduce PRIMEAPE, a multilingual benchmark for evaluating judge verdicts and rationales. PRIMEAPE provides 2,205 response pairs covering 243 instructions in English, French, Spanish, Urdu, Hindi, Norwegian Bokmål, and Yoruba, with 11k human annotations of preferences and rationales across relevance, naturalness, truthfulness, safety, and overall quality. Our evaluation of twelve open- and closed-weight judges reveals that aggregate performance conceals differences across languages and criteria, while requesting rationales does not consistently improve agreement with human preferences. Judges also favor the first position, longer responses, and responses from related models, with effects that vary across criteria and languages. Crucially, judges can justify verdicts that disagree with human preferences while maintaining consistency between their verdicts and rationales. These findings show that consistency with a judge's own verdict does not establish alignment with human judgment. PRIMEAPE enables assessment of both, providing a foundation for more reliable multilingual judges. We release our benchmark and all annotation materials under the CC BY-NC 4.0 license at github.com/Toloka/primeape.

title: Reinforcing Diffusion Models by Instantaneous Trajectory Distribution Matching
summary: Forward diffusion reinforcement learning (RL)---enabling deterministic ODE sampling without trajectory backpropagation---has grown increasingly popular for efficiently aligning diffusion models. However, we reveal that existing methods essentially rely on signed reward-weighted regression (RWR), regressing the trainable policy velocity onto rollouts from a behavior distribution. Unbiased baseline subtraction implicitly assumes that the policy velocity equals the behavior marginal velocity---an idealized assumption violated under classifier-free guidance (CFG) rollouts, offline/off-policy updates, and imperfect online self-consistency. This behavior--policy mismatch breaks baseline invariance and injects baseline-induced gradient drift, destabilizing training. To resolve this issue, we propose Instantaneous Trajectory Distribution Matching (iTDM), taking the infinitesimal limit of Trajectory Distribution Matching toward a time-local reward-guided target via the posterior-score identity to yield a sample-level gradient anchored at the behavior velocity without learning an additional reward-tilted target score. Tracking this velocity with an online auxiliary denoiser guarantees exact baseline invariance at the auxiliary optimum, effectively suppressing baseline drift across both online and offline RL. Extensive experiments across compositional generation, text rendering, and preference alignment show that iTDM achieves state-of-the-art in-domain and out-of-domain performance across group-wise online/offline RL and pairwise offline RL. Notably, on the challenging GenEval2 benchmark, iTDM converges nearly 3\times faster than competing methods while scaling smoothly to 0.87 without collapse. Furthermore, iTDM scales effectively to the 5.6B FLUX.3 model, achieving better performance across both in-domain and unseen metrics. Code is available at https://github.com/Luo-Yihong/iTDM

title: Empirical Margin Sensitivity: An Interventional Neuron-Level Probe of Post-Trained Medical LLMs
summary: Medical post-training raises benchmark accuracy, but accuracy does not show which internal components a model's decisions depend on, or whether components that support one benchmark also support another. We apply the weight-space intervention paradigm of ROME and MEMIT at the granularity of one MLP down-projection column. Our measurement, Empirical Margin Sensitivity (EMS), replaces each coordinate magnitude of a column by its mean while preserving the column's sign pattern and L1 scale, and records the resulting change in the logit margin between the correct option and its hardest-wrong competitor. This isolates the margin's dependence on a column's fine-grained coordinate structure while the column stays in place. We discover high-EMS columns (anchors) on MedQA in ten public checkpoints (four general-purpose bases and six medical post-trained variants) across the Gemma, Llama, Qwen, and AFM families, and measure the same columns on MedMCQA and PubMedQA. Mean-ablating each discovered anchor set lowers MedQA accuracy in all six post-trained models, by 6 to 28 points. In the two pure-SFT checkpoints, crushing anchors raises the PubMedQA margin on correctly answered items (negative EMS), and anchors with this property sit significantly deeper than the same model's other anchors; the four checkpoints trained with RL or mixed recipes show positive PubMedQA EMS and no significant depth shift. The depth association recurs in each of three held-out checkpoints. Because the checkpoints differ in data and pipeline as well as objective, we report these as per-checkpoint observations.

title: NeuroMotion: Aligning EEG to Discrete Motion Primitives for Continuous Motion Decoding
summary: EEG-to-motion decoding remains challenging because noisy scalp EEG is difficult to map directly to continuous kinematics. We present NeuroMotion, a framework that aligns EEG representations to discrete motion primitives for continuous motion decoding across heterogeneous paradigms, including full-body free movement, lower-limb treadmill locomotion, and upper-limb freewill reaching and grasping. A VQ-based motion prior discretizes continuous motion into reusable primitives that serve as both alignment prototypes and intermediate prediction targets. Prototypical and supervised contrastive objectives align EEG embeddings to motion-derived prototypes and organize them according to primitive assignments. An E2M Transformer predicts motion-code sequences from the learned EEG representations, while a final geometric refinement stage improves continuous trajectory reconstruction through motion-level training. Under a last-session test protocol, NeuroMotion achieves the best mean reconstruction performance among the compared EEG decoding baselines across all three datasets, with the clearest gains on full-body motion in both reconstruction accuracy and distribution-level quality. Multi-subject ablations further support the contributions of EEG-to-primitive alignment, token prediction, and refinement. Code is available at https://github.com/Liuyi2351433/NeuroAction.

title: PromptSMC: Enabling Particle Exploration in Flow Matching via LLM-Based Prompt Rejuvenation
summary: This paper is concerned with prompt-image alignment at inference time through exploration of generative trajectories and dynamical prompt rejuvenation. We leverage sequential Monte Carlo (SMC), to offer a gradient-free and principled framework for this purpose through reward-guided trajectory selection. More specifically, we introduce LLM-based prompt rejuvenation, allowing for efficient particle exploration in SMC samplers along the diffusion time in flow matching models. The proposed method, PromptSMC, retains the selected latent states and uses a pretrained LLM to dynamically revise the prompts of duplicated particles under semantic-preservation constraints. These revised prompts induce alternative conditional velocity fields, allowing particles to explore different continuations from a shared intermediate state. The method further uses a reward model to evaluate each particle's alignment with the original prompt, and the resulting scores guide particles through resampling. PromptSMC thus integrates prompt-based exploration with reward-guided sampling, achieving faithful prompt-image alignment without additional noise injection, model training, or reward gradients. Our experiments and ablation studies across multiple benchmarks and backbones demonstrate the effectiveness of the method for text-to-image flow matching. Code is available at https://github.com/shermanlian/PromptSMC.

title: DexDuet: Learning Contact-Preserving Bimanual Dexterity from Human Demonstrations
summary: Human demonstrations provide a rich source of bimanual dexterous skills, yet transferring them to robot hands remains challenging. Existing methods primarily optimize object trajectory tracking, often overlooking how human hands interact with the object. Even with accurate tracking, robots may contact incorrect object parts or slide their fingers, resulting in unstable manipulation. We present DexDuet, a framework that learns contact-preserving bimanual dexterity from a single human demonstration. DexDuet employs two interaction rewards to preserve human hand-object configurations and contacts. To enable coordinated manipulation, we factorize the bimanual policy into two weight-sharing per-hand policies that condition on each other's states. We further propose assisted reference-state initialization (A-RSI), an adaptive curriculum that adjusts object assistance and training starts across demonstration segments to overcome difficult manipulation phases. Across four benchmarks spanning three simulators and five robot embodiments, DexDuet improves object-tracking ADD-AUC by 11 to 41 points over the corresponding baselines while consistently achieving better contact preservation. Notably, among 122 paired runs with comparable object-tracking accuracy, DexDuet preserves the human's contacts better in 117 cases. Code and videos are available at https://rcl-robotics.github.io/Dexduet.io/
